In [[algebraic topology]], a '''simplicial homotopy''' is an analog of a [[homotopy]] between topological spaces for [[simplicial set]]s. Precisely,<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Goerss|first1=Paul G.|url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/837507571|title=Simplicial Homotopy Theory|last2=Jardin|first2=John F.|date=2009|publisher=Birkhäuser Basel|isbn=978-3-0346-0188-7|oclc=837507571}}</ref><sup>pg 23</sup> if
:<math>f, g: X \to Y</math>
are maps between simplicial sets, a simplicial homotopy from ''f'' to ''g'' is a map
:<math>h: X \times \Delta^{1} \to Y</math>
such that the restriction of <math>h</math> along <math>X \simeq X \times \Delta^{0} \overset{0}\hookrightarrow X \times \Delta^{1}</math> is <math>f</math> and the restriction along <math>1</math> is <math>g</math>; see [https://books.google.com/books?id=iFv2BwAAQBAJ&dq=%22simplicial+homotopy%22&pg=PA23]. In particular, <math>f(x) = h(x, 0)</math> and <math>g(x) = h(x, 1)</math> for all ''x'' in ''X''.

Using the adjunction
:<math>\operatorname{Hom}(X \times \Delta^1, Y) = \operatorname{Hom}(\Delta^1 \times X, Y) = \operatorname{Hom}(\Delta^1, \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(X, Y))</math>,
the simplicial homotopy <math>h</math> can also be thought of as a path in the simplicial set <math>\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(X, Y).</math>

A simplicial homotopy is in general not an [[equivalence relation]].<ref>{{harvnb|Joyal|Tierney|2008|loc=§ 2.4.}}</ref> However, if <math>\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(X, Y)</math> is a Kan complex (e.g., if <math>Y</math> is a Kan complex), then a homotopy from <math>f : X \to Y</math> to <math>g : X \to Y</math> is an equivalence relation.<ref name="homotopy">{{harvnb|Joyal|Tierney|2008|loc=§ 3.2.}}</ref> Indeed, a Kan complex is an ∞-groupoid; i.e., every morphism (path) is invertible. Thus, if ''h'' is a homotopy from ''f'' to ''g'', then the inverse of ''h'' is a homotopy from ''g'' to ''f'', establishing that the relation is symmetric. The transitivity holds since a composition is possible.

== Simplicial homotopy equivalence ==
If <math>X</math> is a simplicial set and <math>K</math> a Kan complex, then we form the quotient
:<math>[X, K] = \operatorname{Hom}(X, K)/\sim</math>
where <math>f \sim g</math> means <math>f, g</math> are homotopic to each other. It is the set of the '''simplicial homotopy classes''' of maps from <math>X</math> to <math>K</math>. More generally, Quillen defines homotopy classes using the equivalence relation generated by the homotopy relation.

A map <math>K \to L</math> between Kan complexes is then called a '''simplicial homotopy equivalence''' if the homotopy class <math>[f]</math> of it is bijective; i.e., there is some <math>g</math> such that <math>fg \sim \operatorname{id}_L</math> and <math>gf \sim \operatorname{id}_K</math>.<ref name="homotopy" />

An obvious pointed version of the above consideration also holds.

== Simplicial homotopy group ==
Let <math>S^1</math> be the pushout <math>\Delta^1 \sqcup_{\partial \Delta^1} 1</math> along the boundary <math>S^0 = \partial \Delta^1</math> and <math>S^n = S^1 \wedge \cdots \wedge S^1</math> ''n''-times. Then, as in usual algebraic topology, we define
:<math>\pi_n X = [S^n, X]</math>
for each pointed Kan complex ''X'' and an integer <math>n \ge 0</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Joyal|Tierney|2008|loc=§ 4.2.}}</ref> It is the ''n''-th '''simplicial homotopy group''' of ''X'' (or the set for <math>n = 0</math>). For example, each class in <math>\pi_0 X</math> amounts to a path-connected component of <math>X</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Cisinski|2023|loc=Proposition 3.1.31.}}</ref>

If <math>X</math> is a pointed Kan complex, then the mapping space
:<math>\Omega X = \operatorname{Map}_X(x_0, x_0)</math>
from the base point to itself is also a Kan complex called the [[loop space]] of <math>X</math>. It is also pointed with the base point the identity and so we can iterate: <math>\Omega^n X</math>. It can be shown<ref>{{harvnb|Cisinski|2023|loc=(3.8.8.6)}}</ref>
:<math>\Omega^n X = \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(S^n, X)</math>
as pointed Kan complexes. Thus,
:<math>\pi_n X = \pi_0 \Omega^n X.</math>
Now, we have the identification <math>\pi_0 \operatorname{Map}_C(x, y) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\tau(C)}(x, y)</math> for the [[homotopy category of an ∞-category|homotopy category]] <math>\tau(C)</math> of an ∞-category ''C'' and an [[endomorphism]] group is a group. So, <math>\pi_n X</math> is a group for <math>n \ge 1</math>. By the [[Eckmann-Hilton argument]], <math>\pi_n X</math> is abelian for  <math>n \ge 2</math>.

An analog of [[Whitehead's theorem]] holds: a map <math>f</math> between Kan complexes is a homotopy equivalence if and only if for each choice of base points and each integer <math>n \ge 0</math>, <math>\pi_n(f)</math> is bijective.<ref>{{harvnb|Joyal|Tierney|2008|loc=Theorem 4.4.2.}}</ref>
